lesson.title: Omdat, Maar & Hoewel
lesson.subtitle: cause, contrast and condition — the connectors that change verb order

hook.title: Two Kinds of Join
hook.content: Some connectors keep the main-clause order (maar), some send the verb to the end (omdat, hoewel, als). The connector is the instruction for where the verb goes.

pattern.title: Subordinator or coordinator
pattern.content: Omdat/hoewel/als/wanneer/dat → verb final. Maar/en/of → main-clause order. Ik werk, maar ik ben moe; ik werk omdat ik geld nodig heb.
pattern.trap_note: Want behaves like maar, not like omdat: it keeps main-clause order. This is a common trap for learners who know German.

exercises.prompt: Match each English meaning with its Dutch twin (Omdat, Maar & Hoewel):
exercises.target_answer: omdat, maar, hoewel, als, wanneer, dat
exercises.meaning: because, but, although, if, when, as, when, that (conjunction; relative)
exercises.explanation: These are the anchors of "Omdat, Maar & Hoewel": read each Dutch form through the pattern, not as a new word.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence says: “I come because I have time.”?
options: Ik kom omdat ik tijd heb.
niet Ik kom omdat ik tijd heb.
Ik kom omdat ik tijd heb. (1)
exercises.target_answer: Ik kom omdat ik tijd heb.
exercises.meaning: I come because I have time.
exercises.explanation: “Ik kom omdat ik tijd heb.” is the Dutch form; the other readings bend the pattern of “Omdat, Maar & Hoewel”.

exercises.idea: I work, but I am tired.
cues: It means: I work, but I am tired.
idea_parts: I work, but I am tired.
exercises.target_answer: Ik werk, maar ik ben moe.
exercises.meaning: I work, but I am tired.
exercises.explanation: “Ik werk, maar ik ben moe.” puts the thought together the Dutch way — Subordinator or coordinator.

diagnosis.slip: an English-shaped word order slipped in
diagnosis.cue: Want behaves like maar, not like omdat: it keeps main-clause order. This is a common trap for learners who know German.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentence is built the Dutch way?
options: not Although it rains, go I.
exercises.explanation: “Hoewel het regent, ga ik.” is word-for-word “Although it rains, go I.”. The odd English is the lesson — never a model to produce. Pattern: Subordinator or coordinator.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
cues: It means: If you come, we eat.
exercises.explanation: “Als je komt, eten wij.” reuses only material taught in “Omdat, Maar & Hoewel” — Subordinator or coordinator.
exercises.affirmation: You heard “Als je komt, eten wij.” — a sentence built from the lesson's own Dutch, practising Subordinator or coordinator.

twist.prompt: One more, no safety net — say: “I think that it is good.”
twist.target_answer: Ik denk dat het goed is.
twist.explanation: Dat is a subordinator: the finite verb is goes to the end of its clause.

summary.outcome: Join clauses with the right connector and the right verb position.
summary.takeaway: A connector is a word plus an order rule; learn them together.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on De Brug: Ik Zou Graag….

omdat.context_phrase: Ik kom omdat ik tijd heb.
omdat.context_translation: I come because I have time.
omdat.etymology_derivation: A subordinating conjunction; the verb goes to the end.

maar.context_phrase: Ik werk, maar ik ben moe.
maar.context_translation: I work, but I am tired.
maar.etymology_derivation: A short high-frequency conjunction; the vowel is long.

hoewel.etymology_derivation: hoe + wel, literally 'how well'; a subordinating conjunction.

als.context_phrase: Als het koud is, blijf ik thuis.
als.context_translation: If it is cold, I stay home.
als.etymology_derivation: English as and also are the same root; Dutch als covers if/when/as.

wanneer.etymology_derivation: A compound question word; English when is the short cousin.

dat.etymology_derivation: The neutral demonstrative and conjunction; also the het-relative pronoun.

sch_sh.name: The SCH Bridge
sch_sh.phonetic_rule: English /ʃ/ (sh) corresponds to Dutch /sx/ (sch): ship → schip, shoe → schoen, sheep → schaap.
sch_sh.historical_linguistics: West Germanic *sk stayed a sk-like cluster in Dutch, spelled sch, while English palatalised it to sh.
sch_sh.philological_note: Dutch sch is not English sh; the ch is a voiceless velar fricative. School is a Latin loan shared by both languages.

th_d.name: The TH → D Bridge
th_d.phonetic_rule: English th corresponds to Dutch d: brother → broeder, three → drie, think → denken, thank → danken.
th_d.historical_linguistics: The Germanic dental fricative hardened to a stop in Dutch and German; English kept the fricative.
th_d.philological_note: Weather/weer is cognate but Dutch lost the d, so it is not a th↔d example. Loans such as theater keep t.

f_v.name: The F → V Bridge
f_v.phonetic_rule: English f often corresponds to Dutch v: father → vader, foot → voet, fish → vis.
f_v.historical_linguistics: Dutch voiced West Germanic f to v in many positions; English kept the voiceless consonant.
f_v.philological_note: Northern Dutch often devoices v to [f], especially in vr-/vl- clusters and word-finally; the spelling keeps the historical v.

s_z.name: The S → Z Bridge
s_z.phonetic_rule: English s often corresponds to Dutch z: sun → zon, sea → zee, salt → zout.
s_z.historical_linguistics: Dutch voiced West Germanic s before vowels; English kept s.
s_z.philological_note: Clusters sn/sm/sl keep s (sneeuw, smal, slapen); loans such as school and straat also keep s.

gh_ch.name: The GH → CH Bridge
gh_ch.phonetic_rule: English gh corresponds to Dutch ch: night → nacht, light → licht, right → recht, eight → acht.
gh_ch.historical_linguistics: English gh and Dutch ch descend from a shared velar fricative; English vocalised or lost it, Dutch kept it.
gh_ch.philological_note: Dutch g is the voiced partner of ch. The two are different sounds, not spelling variants.

vowel_ij.name: The IJ Bridge
vowel_ij.phonetic_rule: Dutch ij is /ɛi/ and often answers to English i/y: ice → ijs, wine → wijn, five → vijf.
vowel_ij.historical_linguistics: The digraph ij spells a Dutch diphthong; English orthography kept a different vowel from the same Germanic stock.
vowel_ij.philological_note: IJ is two letters but one sound. It is not English /aɪ/.

vowel_ui.name: The UI Bridge
vowel_ui.phonetic_rule: Dutch ui is /œy/ and often answers to English ou/ow: house → huis, mouse → muis, out → uit.
vowel_ui.historical_linguistics: Dutch ui spells a front rounded diphthong with no close English equivalent; the English spelling twin is a memory hook.
vowel_ui.philological_note: Do not pronounce ui as two English beats; it is one gliding vowel.

vowel_oe.name: The OE Bridge
vowel_oe.phonetic_rule: Dutch oe is /u/ and often answers to English oo/u in spelling: book → boek, foot → voet, good → goed.
vowel_oe.historical_linguistics: The Dutch digraph oe spells a long /u/; English oo spells several different vowels, so this is a spelling/cognacy bridge.
vowel_oe.philological_note: Dutch oe is /u/, not the /ʊ/ of English book. Read the Dutch spelling and use the Dutch sound.

g_y.name: The G / Y Bridge
g_y.phonetic_rule: English g and some y words correspond to voiced Dutch g: gold → goud, good → goed, yellow → geel.
g_y.historical_linguistics: Dutch kept a velar fricative where English kept a stop or palatalised to y. English year/jaar is y↔j, not y↔g.
g_y.philological_note: Dutch g is a fricative, never the English stop in 'good'.
